common_name: Olympic Flame Skimmia (AGM Female Evergreen Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant a male Skimmia pollinator nearby in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in shade; this RHS Award of Garden Merit female clone needs cross-pollination to set its heavy red berry crop.

directions: An RHS Award of Garden Merit holder, this female selection opens deep red winter flower buds into conical clusters of fragrant, pale pink spring flowers that draw early pollinators, followed by a heavy set of glossy red berries once a male Skimmia is planted nearby. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full or partial shade, since both strong sun and dry soil cause leaf scorch and yellowing. Mulch yearly to hold moisture and soil acidity, and limit pruning to shaping right after flowering, since fruit forms on growth from the prior season. Its rounded, dense habit and long-lasting berries make it a strong choice for a shaded foundation bed or woodland border.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this white-flowered form shows none of the pink blush or red veining typical of the species, so it stands out best against a dark evergreen backdrop.

directions: This selection replaces the pink-flushed, red-veined bells typical of redvein enkianthus with clean, greenish-white to pure white blooms, hanging in clusters along tiered branches in late spring without losing the species' strong orange-to-scarlet fall color. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade alongside rhododendrons and azaleas, which share the same root and soil requirements. The layered, horizontal branching gives the shrub structural interest through winter even without flowers, and it is best sited where the pale blooms show up against darker evergreen neighbors. Prune only right after flowering to remove dead or crossing wood, since next year's buds form on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this exceptionally slow-growing dwarf form of white enkianthus tops out at roughly 2 feet, making it suitable for rock gardens and small foundation beds where the full-size species would be too large.

directions: A true dwarf form of white enkianthus, 'Compactus' grows at a fraction of the species' rate and stays under two feet tall even at maturity, forming a dense, rounded mound of fine-textured foliage. Small, pure white, urn-shaped flowers dangle beneath the branches just before or as the leaves emerge in spring, followed by the same reliable red-to-orange fall color the species is known for, concentrated on a much smaller frame. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, matching the conditions preferred by azaleas and rhododendrons, and avoid soils that dry out or run alkaline. Because of its slow growth and compact habit, it fits well in rock gardens, trough plantings, or the front edge of an ericaceous border where a full-size enkianthus would overwhelm the space.
